The Tristan chord, F–B–D♯–G♯, sounds in bar 2 of the prelude to Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde and does not resolve by the usual rules; Wagner scholars label the opening motive “Longing”. Debussy turned it into a syncopated arpeggio in Golliwogg’s Cakewalk, and Berg quoted the Tristan motif in the last movement of the Lyric Suite.

The bass descends through a fourth and then repeats. In Purcell’s When I am laid in earth it fills the descent from G to D with every semitone, and Dido sings her farewell over it. Monteverdi, Biber, Bach and Beethoven also built pieces on the descending ground.

La Folia is an old Iberian dance tune with a standard harmonic scheme. Vivaldi’s Trio Sonata RV 63 begins with the first violin stating the tune slowly in D minor; in the variations the violins play fast running figures. Corelli, Marais, Geminiani, C. P. E. Bach, Liszt and Rachmaninoff also used it.

Beethoven’s tune in the finale of the Ninth Symphony, first performed in Vienna on 7 May 1824, sets Schiller’s An die Freude. It begins on a repeated note and moves by step. The finale theme of Brahms’s First Symphony recalls it, the Council of Europe adopted the melody as its wordless anthem in 1972, and in Berlin in 1989 Bernstein conducted the finale with Freiheit sung in place of Freude.

In the third movement of Mahler’s First Symphony the round Frère Jacques (Bruder Martin) is played in D minor by a solo double bass over a timpani ostinato, and a canon is built from it. The bassoon and cellos join the round. The Beatles sang it in the backing vocals of Paperback Writer in 1966.
